title: Teaching on Purpose #19: Hinge Questions
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: In this installment of Teaching on Purpose, Adam Kohlbeck writes up his conversation with headteacher and English teacher Chris Passey about the hinge question, a quick whole-class diagnostic check placed at the point in a lesson where the next step depends on the answer. Passey stresses that a hinge is a fork in the road rather than a simple forwards or backwards choice, and that every wrong option should be built to reveal a specific misconception. They work through examples from Blake's London and The Woman in Black, show how a written version at the start of a lesson doubles as retrieval practice, and describe low-tech response methods such as mini whiteboards and ABCD cards, always with simultaneous reveal and never hands up. Passey also lists when he would not use a hinge question, including straight after teaching, with creative or evaluative questions, when pupils' emotional needs come first, and when the lesson is already full of checks.
points: A hinge question belongs mid-lesson at a moment where pupils' answers can still change what the teacher does next; one placed at the end is too late to act on.
Each distractor should map to a real misconception, so a deliberately silly wrong answer wastes the diagnostic value of the question.
Responses should be collected simultaneously on mini whiteboards, ABCD cards or fingers, because hands up shows only what the most confident pupils think.
A planned set of responses (move on, split the room, or re-explain with a concrete example) lets teachers abandon the plan calmly when evidence demands it.
Barometer students can quietly stand in for the whole class, which gives teachers a rose-tinted view of learning.
quotes: A hinge question is a quick, whole-class diagnostic check placed at exactly one of those moments. As Chris put it, it does what it says on the tin.

This matters because a hinge question that sits at the end of a lesson is too late to act on. It has to sit in the middle, at the point where the information it gives you can still change what you do next.

Chris also warned against including a deliberately silly wrong answer. If one option is obviously ridiculous, say a handbag in my animal question, you lose the chance to diagnose a real misconception. Every option should tell you something.
The first is never hands up, because all that tells you is what your five most confident pupils think.
The strongest lessons are often the ones where the teacher has planned for the possibility that pupils will not have got it, so there is no panic, just options:
Straight after new content has been taught. There is nothing to diagnose yet, and the effects of recency will make it look as though everyone has got it.
The problem comes when one answer quietly becomes the judgement for the whole class.
